summary: This experimental document defines a convergence layer for CCNx and NDN over IEEE 802.15.4 LoWPANs. It specifies a new frame format for the small MTU, changes to TLV header formats, new 6LoWPAN dispatch types and use of 6LoWPAN fragmentation.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny low-power gadgets can only send tiny packets. This experiment shows how to squeeze name-based network messages into those little packets.

questions: how does stateful compression work in icn
subtitle: Squeezing content-based networking into the tiniest wireless devices.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) protocols like NDN and CCNx use verbose Type-Length-Value headers designed for flexible, extensible communication. IEEE 802.15.4 wireless links in IoT devices have tiny maximum frame sizes (127 bytes total, 102 available for payload), leaving little room for ICN protocol overhead.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9139 defines a convergence layer for ICN over constrained Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (LoWPANs). It compresses ICN headers using compact bit fields for optional fields, elides common values, and employs both stateless and stateful compression schemes to minimize packet size while preserving compatibility with existing 6LoWPAN technologies.
tldr.outcome: ICN messages can now travel over IEEE 802.15.4 networks with significantly reduced packet size, lower power consumption, and shortened transmission times. This is experimental research work that demonstrates the feasibility of name-based networking on severely resource-constrained devices.

today: RFC 9139 is an Experimental specification, published in November 2021 by the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and represents ongoing research into applying ICN principles to resource-constrained IoT networks.

sections.title: ICN on Constrained Networks
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking (ICN) offers advantages for Internet of Things (IoT) deployments: content is accessed by name rather than host address, allowing caching and resilience to network failures. However, ICN protocols like Named Data Networking (NDN) and Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) were designed for general-purpose networks and use verbose Type-Length-Value (TLV) header formats.

IEEE 802.15.4 wireless links used in low-power IoT devices have a maximum frame size of 127 bytes. With 25 bytes for link-layer headers and optional security, only about 81 bytes remain for ICN protocol headers, signatures, and content. The header verbosity of ICN protocols severely limits the effective payload per packet.

This document specifies a convergence layer for ICN over IEEE 802.15.4 LoWPANs that applies compression techniques similar to those used in 6LoWPAN (IPv6 over LoWPAN) to reduce ICN header overhead and improve the effective throughput on constrained links.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny wireless devices want to use a name-based networking system, but the protocol is too wordy for such small packets. This RFC shows how to shorten the protocol so it fits.

sections.title: Compression Techniques
sections.content:
ICN LoWPAN employs three complementary compression strategies. First, it provides a convergence layer that maps ICN packets onto IEEE 802.15.4 frames using the 6LoWPAN dispatch framework. This allows ICN, IPv6, and other protocols to coexist on the same wireless medium by using dispatch types to identify the payload type.

Stateless compression reduces header overhead without requiring shared state. Compact bit fields indicate which optional Type-Length-Value fields are present. Default values are assumed for many fields (such as a HopLimit of 255 for NDN), and the bit field order mirrors the packet structure to avoid repeating field lengths. For example, fixed-length fields like the Nonce in NDN have their type and length removed entirely.

Stateful compression uses two techniques: LoWPAN-local state allows context identifiers (CIDs) to replace frequently appearing prefixes, suffixes, or metadata throughout the local network; en route state replaces the full name in Data responses with a single-byte HopID, since the return name either matches or prefixes the original Interest name. Forwarders store these HopIDs in extensions to the Pending Interest Table to enable hop-by-hop name compression.
sections.plainLanguage: The compression works by dropping repetitive information, using defaults instead of explicit values, and replacing long names with short codes. Some tricks require nodes to remember what was sent before.

sections.title: Frame Format and TLV Encoding
sections.content:
ICN LoWPAN uses a new Type-Length-Value encoding for compressed messages that is more space-efficient than the original NDN and CCNx TLV schemes. Instead of fixed-size markers for the number of following bytes, this encoding uses Self-Delimiting Numeric Values (SDNVs) where a single bit indicates if more bytes follow. This reduces the overhead for encoding field lengths and types.

For example, the value 253 requires 3 bytes in the original NDN encoding (0xFD 0x00 0xFD) but only 2 bytes in the SDNV format (0x81 0x7D). Similarly, 2^16 needs 5 bytes normally but only 3 bytes with SDNVs.

Name components are compressed by encoding the length of two consecutive NameComponents into one byte using nibbles (4-bit values). Each nibble holds the length of one component, limiting each to 15 bytes but eliminating the separate length field for each component. A length of 0 marks the end of the name.

The dispatch header includes bits indicating which optional fields are present, the message type (Interest or Data), and whether compression was applied. Extended dispatch formats and extension bytes allow for future enhancements.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbers are encoded with a special trick where a single bit says if more bytes follow. Names are squeezed by packing two length fields into one byte. A bit field says which optional parts are included.

sections.title: Per-Protocol Compression Rules
sections.content:
RFC 9139 defines separate compression rules for NDN and CCNx Interest and Data messages, since their header structures differ. For NDN Interests, the outermost message type field is removed, the name is compressed per the name encoding rules, fixed-length fields like Nonce (4 bytes) and HopLimit (1 byte) have their type and length elided, and a Nonce and InterestLifetime are moved to the end of the message.

For NDN Data messages, the message type, name, MetaInfo type, and signature type fields are removed; the FreshnessPeriod is encoded as a compressed 1-byte time-code and moved to the end. Additional bits in the dispatch header indicate the presence of optional fields like FinalBlockId, ContentType, and KeyLocator.

CCNx messages use analogous rules adapted to the fixed-size CCNx TLV header (2 bytes per field). The version and packet type are elided and assumed from the dispatch bits. Both Interest and Content Object messages can omit the fixed header version, packet type, and message type fields.

If a message contains TLV fields not covered by the compression rules, it must be sent uncompressed to preserve all information. The document defines dispatch extensions to allow future compression strategies to be negotiated and deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message type has specific rules for what fields to drop and what to abbreviate. If a message has something unusual, it is sent the long way instead of trying to compress it.

sections.title: Security and Robustness
sections.content:
Fragmentation of ICN packets to fit into the small IEEE 802.15.4 frame size requires buffering all fragments until reassembly is complete. On memory-constrained devices, a flood of fragments from different packets can exhaust buffer space, causing a denial of service. Implementers are urged to use appropriate buffer replacement strategies and may consider minimal fragment forwarding (RFC 8930) to prevent buffer saturation.

Stateful compression using ephemeral HopIDs creates a potential attack surface: an attacker can send forged Interests with fake HopIDs to exhaust the available HopID space, denying compression service for legitimate traffic. Link-layer security mechanisms should be deployed to restrict frame acceptance and prevent forged packets. IEEE 802.15.4 itself provides optional frame encryption and authentication to protect against these threats.

The compression scheme itself does not introduce new cryptographic vulnerabilities; ICN messages preserve their original signatures and security envelopes. However, implementers must ensure that the decompression of time values does not cause security violations if a compressed time value underflows to a smaller value than intended.
sections.plainLanguage: Memory can run out if too many fragments arrive at once. Attackers could send fake messages to exhaust the HopID pool. Link-layer security helps prevent these problems.
